title: New men left to find their parts
summary: New saxophone players had no one to show them the unwritten parts and sat lost until Harry Carney or others helped; Ben Webster was liked.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: They didn't have no arguments in --
In those days.
No. In those days.
No.

In the later days. Because a guy would come in the saxophone section, a new man come in there, and he'd just be setting there. A guy wouldn't tell him what he'd be playing next or nothing. He'd just be sitting there. He'd be lost. By the time he'd be getting into the number, he'd be looking for the music, we done finished.
(Laughter)
(Laughter)
Well, would you mind telling me why nobody ever helped the new guy?
No, they never helped him.
Well, why is that?
Well, I don't know. The -- they never felt like it was their duty.
(Unintelligible) An intruder or something?
No, they didn't feel like it was their duty to be telling him and helping him, because the majority of the music -- you see, Duke didn't write all of the music out.
I know.
He would give you certain notes, and you'd play a certain part like this, on the piano, note for note, and it wasn't written out.
Yeah.

And when the new guy come in there, he'd have a piece of music, and he'd have a great big blank space, and things, and the guy wouldn't know what to be playing, you know. And the guys would keep on playing their parts. They wouldn't even hunch him or nothing. And the guy'd just be sitting there, till he'd catch on.
Well, is that because the band just felt like they were they, and there was nobody quite like them
and that was it. And you either sank or swam, huh?
(Laughter)
Well, I don't know what the idea was.
Well, what would you do in the trumpet section?
Well, I'd help a guy when he come in.
You would help a guy.
Yeah.
Yeah.
But it only went on down there in the read section.
Oh, I see. Isn't that funny. Well, wouldn't Ellington do anything?
No.
Well, why wouldn't Ellington do anything?
Ellington didn't pay anybody no mind. He just -- it would depend on the guy catching on. And Harry would help a guy, maybe.
Yeah.
If he was over next to Harry.
Yeah.
Maybe Harry would help him. But he had to save him -- I mean, if he wasn't over there next to Harry.
(Laughter)
Because he'd be sitting up there like
a dummy.
(Laughter)

Oh, gosh, that's funny. Well, when that would happen to a guy, say like Ben Webster, now that must have been funny, because Ben Webster is not a guy that's going to take kindly to being dropped in the ocean, is he?
Well, they liked Ben.
Yeah. Yeah.
And --
I guess Ben knew what they were blowing anyway --
Yeah.
-- before he ever came in.
Ben knew what -- kinda what they were doing --
Yeah.
-- before he came in the band. And Johnny liked Ben.
Harry loved Ben, didn't he?
Yeh. Uh-huh. Well, the majority of them in the band liked Ben.
Yeah.
So he was just like one of the members when he come in there.
Yeah.
So he didn't have a rough time.
No. No, that's right. So, well that thing you're talking about, that applied to the poor guy off-stage, too, didn't it?
Oh, yeah.
I mean --
I don't imagine too much off stage, as it happened when he got ready to go on that stage. When he got ready to go on, they just didn't pay him any mind. Maybe they figured it was Duke's job.
Yeah. I see what you mean, yeah. Everybody was just minding their business.

Yeah. Everybody was minding their business, playing their horn, playing their part. You know, but I'd show the guy how to get the music, because the music was -- sometimes they didn't have much music up there.
I know. So, then, too -- I mean, if it comes to a record session, then a lot of that music is written out, ready to make a record. I mean, it must be rough on any guy that was new in the band then.
